catalog_quote: In regard to the matter of tones and stress, the principal stress is laid on the syllable containing the theme or root, as in the sentence, na-yi-nu a-hoi-td (v) em? A-hoi-tai. Kade. Your wife she pretty is ? (Is your wife pretty ?) She pretty is I love (She is pretty, I love her). The stress in the first word is laid on the sylla- ble yif in the second word on the syllable hoi, in the third word oti the syllable hoi, in the fourth word on the syllable de, the emphasised syllable being in each case that which is operative, conveying the theme or root of the word. Other than this, there is no system of tonal modification, and the only emphasis is that which the natural exigencies of conversation demand, and it may therefore be called natural emphasis.

new_statements.relation_note: Catalog record has an empty rule. This work supplies content: the language is tonal, and stress is only emphatic/mobile (utterance-level), with no fixed word position; the only positional claim is Hodson 1906's root-syllable stress, reported secondhand.
new_statements.rule_in_words: Thadou has three contrastive tones (rising, level, falling) and 'a stress', but the only stress described is emphatic: it can be placed on any utterance and its position shifts according to what is emphasized, so there is no fixed word-stress position. The thesis secondhand-quotes Hodson (1906) as putting 'principal stress' on the root/theme syllable (a morphologically determined placement), which the author treats as Hodson's substitute for a tone analysis. Ch. 5 (p. 108 area) adds that the adjectival prefix /ə/ is unstressed.
new_statements.exceptions: Hodson 1906 (quoted p. 20): principal stress on the root/theme syllable; adjectival prefix /ə-/ said to be unstressed (ch. 5)
new_statements.identity_note: Both theses describe Thadou (Thadou-Kuki) of Manipur, India, i.e. the Glottolog thad1238 variety; the 2014 thesis says its data came from native speakers recorded in isolation and citation forms (p. 65). Hyman's 'Kuki-Thaadow' material (held by the project from the earlier reading, not among the listed works) is the same language under a different spelling.

readall_conflicts: No direct contradiction among the works opened. Haokip 2014 (JNU) treats Thadou as a pure three-tone language and never mentions stress; Haokip 2007 (NEHU) lists 'stress' as a suprasegmental phoneme beside tone but describes it only as emphatic stress that can fall anywhere depending on emphasis, i.e. no fixed word-stress rule. The one positional claim, Hodson 1906's 'principal stress is laid on the syllable containing the theme or the root', is quoted secondhand in Haokip 2007 (p. 20) and is framed there as a pre-tonal description that missed the tones; it is not endorsed. Haokip 2008 could not be opened, so whether it makes a stress claim is unknown. The two theses also differ on the tone inventory (2007: rising/level/falling; 2014: H, LH, L with underlying L/H per Haokip 2008), but that is tone, not stress.
